## 1\. A fixed three-actuator family

Consider

\[
\boxed{
\mathcal F_3=
\{(e_1,e_2),(e_2,e_3),(e_3,e_1)\}.
}
\]

Every pair has a nonzero integer frequency, a rational polarization and \(a\cdot p=0\)\. No spatial frequency depends on \(\nu,K\) or the target accuracy.

Let \(U_i(s)\) be the exact inviscid linear velocity propagator for actuator \(i\), with its unknown admissible static calibration and arbitrary phase. The parameter \(s\) is the integrated nominal pulse strength.

Define the Fourier projection

\[
Q_R f=\sum_{\substack{k\in\mathbb Z^3\setminus\{0\}\\|k|_\infty\le R}}
\widehat f(k)e^{2\pi i k\cdot x}.
\]

Fix \(R=256\)\.

### Theorem: uniform low-block evacuation

For every rational \(0<\zeta\le1/2\), an explicitly computable integer \(s\), with

\[
s\le C\zeta^{-3},
\]

satisfies

\[
\boxed{
\sup_{\text{all admissible calibrations}}
\left\|Q_{256}U_3(s)U_2(s)U_1(s)Q_{256}
\right\|_{L^2\to L^2}
\le\zeta.
}
\tag{1}
\]

Here \(C\) is an absolute computable constant. The theorem includes every divergence-free polarization, arbitrary phases and independently chosen calibration errors.

### Proof: the unique Fourier path

Take an input frequency \(k=(k_1,k_2,k_3)\) and an output frequency \(k'=(k'_1,k'_2,k'_3)\)\.

The first actuator changes only the first Fourier coordinate, the second only the second, and the third only the third. Therefore exactly one sequence of intermediate frequencies can connect \(k\) to \(k'\)\:

\[
\begin{aligned}
q_0&=(k_1,k_2,k_3),\\
q_1&=(k'_1,k_2,k_3),\\
q_2&=(k'_1,k'_2,k_3),\\
q_3&=(k'_1,k'_2,k'_3).
\end{aligned}
\tag{2}
\]

The matrix element of the three-pulse product is exactly

\[
\Pi_{q_3}U_3\Pi_{q_2}\,
\Pi_{q_2}U_2\Pi_{q_1}\,
\Pi_{q_1}U_1\Pi_{q_0}.
\tag{3}
\]

There is no sum over alternative paths. This eliminates the high-frequency intermediate cancellation problem for this three-actuator word.

The three nominal coupling coefficients along (2) are

\[
\boxed{k_2,\qquad k_3,\qquad k'_1.}
\tag{4}
\]

Suppose all three vanish. Then \(k=(k_1,0,0)\), and the first actuator has exactly zero coupling because its actual polarization is perpendicular to \(e_1\)\. Hence it cannot change \(k_1\)\. A nonzero matrix element would require \(k'_1=k_1\), contradicting \(k'_1=0\) unless \(k=0\), which is excluded.

Thus every nonzero matrix element has at least one stage whose nominal coupling is a nonzero integer.

## 2\. Implementing the three shears in the nonlinear equation

The low-block theorem can be made into a physical, calibration-robust controller over a finite interval while retaining polynomial resources.

Choose

\[
\zeta=\min\left\{\frac18,\frac{\nu}{100K}\right\},
\]

and compute \(s\) from (7).

Define

\[
L=(1+2^{34}s)^3,\qquad K_0=K.
\]

For stages \(i=1,2,3\), compute

\[
K_i=8LK_{i-1},
\qquad
E_i=\nu K_i+2^{30}K_i^2,
\]

\[
\boxed{
D_i=
\left\lceil
2^{50}\left(
1+L^2K_{i-1}+\frac{E_i}{\zeta K}
\right)
\right\rceil,
\qquad
\delta_i=D_i^{-1}.
}
\tag{8}
\]

Define disjoint pulse intervals by

\[
t_0=0,\quad
I_i=[t_{i-1},t_{i-1}+\delta_i],
\quad
t_i=t_{i-1}+2\delta_i.
\]

Thus every pulse is followed by a zero-control gap of the same duration.

With

\[
h(z)=140z^3(1-z)^3,
\]

the nominal envelope is

\[
f_i(t)=
\begin{cases}
sD_i h(D_i(t-t_{i-1})),&t\in I_i,\\
0,&\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\]

These are nonnegative degree-six rational polynomials and globally \(C^2\)\.

### Uniform nonlinear continuation through the pulses

The accepted BCA polynomial directional hierarchy applies to every actual calibrated shear, because its polarization remains perpendicular to its fixed frequency.

The definition (8) is sufficiently conservative to give

\[
\sup_{t_{i-1}\le t\le t_i}
\|u(t)\|_{H^3}\le K_i.
\tag{9}
\]

The nonlinear equation therefore has a unique strong solution through all three pulse intervals and gaps, uniformly over initial states and calibration choices.

Let \(u_i=u(t_i)\) and denote the physical-versus-inviscid stage error by

\[
r_i=u_i-U_i(s)u_{i-1}.
\]

Duhamel's formula, \(L^2\)\-unitarity of \(U_i\), and the \(H^3\) bounds yield

\[
\|r_i\|_2\le2\delta_i E_i
\le\frac{2\zeta K}{2^{50}}.
\]

Thus

\[
u_3=U_3U_2U_1u_0+U_3U_2r_1+U_3r_2+r_3,
\]

and the cumulative physical approximation error is less than \(\zeta K\)\.

Meanwhile, the initial high-frequency tail satisfies

\[
\|(I-Q_{256})u_0\|_2
\le\frac{K}{257^3}.
\]

Combining these estimates with (1) gives the uniform physical conclusion

\[
\boxed{
\|Q_{256}u(t_3)\|_2
\le2\zeta K+\frac{K}{257^3}
\le\frac{\nu}{50}+\frac{K}{257^3}.
}
\tag{10}
\]

This is a proved finite-time low-mode suppression result for the actual nonlinear equation, not merely its inviscid linearization.
